stories.headline: S&P 500, DOW SNAP THREE-DAY SKID AS YIELDS AND OIL COOL OFF
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.46% to 7,666.60 and the Dow added 0.56% to 53,061.95, both snapping three-day losing streaks, while Nvidia rallied more than 3% to lift the megacaps; the Nasdaq 100 lagged, finishing essentially flat near 29,050 even as the broader Nasdaq Composite gained 0.45%.
stories.explain: Wednesday's bounce came almost entirely from Treasury yields and oil pausing their recent surge rather than any new bullish catalyst, which is why small-caps (Russell 2000 +1.1%) outperformed the rate-sensitive Nasdaq 100: a stalling discount rate helps beaten-down cyclical and value names proportionally more than it helps mega-cap growth stocks that had already been bid up on AI capex expectations.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD TOUCHES 4.818%, HIGHEST SINCE NOVEMBER 2023, BEFORE EASING
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield hit an intraday high of 4.818% Wednesday before settling near 4.79%, a level not seen since November 2023, as markets now price roughly 60 bps of additional Fed tightening through year-end following last week's hawkish Fed commentary.
stories.explain: The 10-year yield embeds both the market's expected path for the fed funds rate and a term premium investors demand for holding longer-duration debt; when oil-driven inflation expectations rise at the same time the Fed signals it isn't done hiking, both components climb together, which is exactly why the note broke above its late-2023 high even though the Fed hasn't moved rates yet this cycle.

stories.headline: OIL HOLDS NEAR FIVE-WEEK HIGH AS U.S.-IRAN CONFLICT KEEPS STRAIT OF HORMUZ AT RISK
stories.body: Brent crude added 0.23% to $94.86 a barrel and WTI held near $91 after Tuesday's 5.2% spike, the biggest one-day gain in five weeks, following fresh U.S. strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz after Iran attacked tankers transiting the waterway.
stories.explain: About one-fifth of the world's seaborne crude passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so oil traders price in the probability of disruption immediately rather than waiting for an actual supply interruption; that risk premium is why Brent is up more than 13% over the past month even though no sustained physical flow of oil has yet been cut off.

stories.headline: COMMERCE SECRETARY SIGNALS SEMICONDUCTOR TARIFF FRAMEWORK IS COMING
stories.body: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told CNBC the administration is finalizing a tariff framework specifically targeting semiconductors, and that chipmakers are already aware duties are on the way, adding a new cost variable for an industry already absorbing higher energy and input costs from the Iran-driven oil spike.
stories.explain: Tariff pass-through depends on how concentrated the supply chain is: semiconductors have few substitute suppliers in the near term, so importers have limited ability to source around a new duty, meaning a larger share of any chip tariff is likely to show up in downstream electronics and AI-hardware prices rather than being absorbed by manufacturer margins.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS TOWARD $4,320 DESPITE ESCALATING IRAN CONFLICT
stories.body: Gold fell roughly 0.7% to around $4,320 an ounce Wednesday even as U.S.-Iran hostilities intensified, a break from bullion's usual safe-haven script, as the pop in real yields tied to hawkish Fed repricing outweighed the war-risk premium that would typically lift gold.
stories.explain: Gold carries no yield, so its opportunity cost is set by real (inflation-adjusted) interest rates; when nominal yields rise faster than inflation expectations, as they have this week on Fed repricing, the real rate climbs and holding non-yielding bullion becomes relatively less attractive versus Treasurys, overpowering the safe-haven bid from the Iran conflict.

stories.headline: NCAA WINS FOURTH STRAIGHT ELIGIBILITY APPEAL AS COURT RULINGS KEEP SHIFTING ROSTERS
stories.body: The NCAA won another eligibility appeal Tuesday, its fourth in recent weeks after prior wins in Colorado, Ohio and Tennessee, even as Syracuse guard Amarri Monroe was separately granted a temporary restraining order in New York making him eligible this season; Michigan's five-star freshman Brandon McCoy Jr. will miss the entire 2026-27 season with a torn ACL.

stories.headline: CLIPPERS, RAPTORS IN TRADE TALKS FOR KAWHI LEONARD
stories.body: The Clippers and Raptors are in extended discussions on a deal for All-NBA forward Kawhi Leonard as the offseason reshuffle continues; elsewhere, Russell Westbrook joined new startup league Project B as chief strategy officer weeks after retiring as a player, while Rockets guard Fred VanVleet and Kings guard Zach LaVine both opted into their 2026-27 player options.

stories.headline: LIONS PLACE ISIAH PACHECO ON IR AS TEAMS SET FINAL ROSTERS FOR SEPT. 9 OPENERS
stories.body: Detroit placed running back Isiah Pacheco on injured reserve with an MCL sprain and back injury suffered in camp, while Odell Beckham made the Giants' initial 53-man roster and 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey returned to practice for the first time since Aug. 8, as teams finalize rosters ahead of the Sept. 9 season kickoff.

stories.headline: WEEK 1 KICKS OFF THURSDAY, HEADLINED BY KIFFIN'S LSU DEBUT AGAINST CLEMSON
stories.body: The 2026 season's full Week 1 slate begins Thursday and runs through Monday, headlined by Lane Kiffin's debut as No. 11 LSU's coach against Clemson, plus Boise State at Oregon, Notre Dame opening against Wisconsin, and No. 5 Texas hosting Texas State.

sports.detail: Third-year coach Jedd Fisch's Huskies host Washington State in the Apple Cup on Sept. 5 to open the season, the first of four straight September home games at Husky Stadium; junior QB Demond Williams returns after completing nearly 70% of his passes for 3,065 yards and 25 touchdowns last season.

Danny Sprinkle's program hosts four-star 2027 guard Jimmie Haywood, a Seattle native, on an official visit Sept. 5, with five-star forward Ahmed Nur set to visit Sept. 6 as Washington works to rebuild its recruiting pipeline after a 16-17 finish.

The defending Super Bowl champions finalized their 53-man roster after going winless in the preseason; Seattle signed CB Trevon Diggs and agreed to terms with Terrion Arnold, though Arnold faces a likely commissioner's exempt-list placement. Seattle opens Sept. 9 at home against New England in a Super Bowl rematch, without RB Kenneth Walker III, who departed for Kansas City.

Coming off a 60-win season, Detroit fully guaranteed backup center Paul Reed's $5.6M deal for 2026-27, contingent on Jalen Duren re-signing; the Pistons still need to finalize a long-term extension with forward Ausar Thompson before training camp opens.

Seattle beat Boston 9-6 Tuesday behind Lazaro Montes' home run in his MLB debut and a three-run shot from Randy Arozarena, snapping a five-game skid; the Mariners (64-73) are back at Fenway Park today, first pitch 4:10 PM ET (2:10 PM MT) — likely still underway as this brief publishes.

watchlist: FOMC meeting mid-September — futures price roughly 60 bps of additional tightening through year-end after last week's hawkish Fed commentary
Brent crude near $95 on the U.S.-Iran conflict — watch for further Strait of Hormuz disruption or a new round of strikes
Semiconductor tariff framework expected from the Commerce Department — Secretary Lutnick says chipmakers are aware duties are coming
Huskies open the season vs. Washington State (Apple Cup) — Saturday, Sept. 5, Husky Stadium
CFB Week 1 headliners: Lane Kiffin's LSU debut vs. Clemson, and Boise State at Oregon — Sept. 3-7

deepDive.title: Why the Strait of Hormuz Moves Oil Before a Single Barrel Stops Flowing
content: Today's brief shows Brent crude sitting near $94.86 and WTI holding around $91, both elevated even though U.S.-Iran hostilities near the Strait of Hormuz haven't actually cut off a meaningful volume of crude. That gap between price and physical disruption is the story: markets are pricing risk, not just realized supply, and understanding how they do that explains why oil can jump 5% in a single session on strikes hundreds of miles from any producing well.

The mechanism is straightforward once you separate spot flow from expected flow. Roughly one-fifth of the world's seaborne crude and a similar share of global LNG transits the Strait, a chokepoint just 21 miles wide at its narrowest, with a shipping lane on each side barely two miles across. Traders don't need Iran to actually mine or block the strait to reprice oil — they only need the probability of disruption to rise, because futures contracts settle on where the market expects prices to be at delivery, not on today's undisrupted flow. A credible military escalation raises that probability instantly, and the futures curve moves with it.

This is the same dynamic that drove 2019's Abqaiq attack, which knocked out roughly 5% of global oil supply for days and sent Brent up nearly 15% in a single session, and the 1980s Tanker War, when Iran and Iraq attacked shipping in the Gulf for years without ever fully closing the strait — prices stayed elevated the entire time purely on sustained disruption risk. What's easy to miss is that this risk premium can unwind just as fast as it builds: once a ceasefire or de-escalation looks credible, the premium can evaporate within days even if nothing about physical supply has changed, which is why oil-driven inflation scares can reverse quickly and catch traders offside in both directions.

For markets right now, that risk premium is doing double duty: it's propping up headline inflation readings the Fed will see before its September meeting, and it's part of why the 10-year yield pushed to a nearly three-year high this week. If the conflict de-escalates, expect both oil and the inflation narrative behind the Fed's hawkish tilt to cool quickly — but if strikes continue or shipping insurers start pricing in real transit risk through the strait, the premium embedded in today's $91 WTI print could still have room to grow before it breaks.
